pages.text:
DoorDash Debuts Returns Program Amid New Retail Partnerships
DoorDash launched a returns program along with an expansion of its retail marketplace, according to a Wednesday (Sept. 30) press release.
The expansion involves partnerships in the apparel, beauty and home spaces, with Macy’s, Anthropologie, The North Face, Vans and Timberland now available options to customers, the release said.
“This is what we mean by the mall in your pocket: the brands you already know and trust, on the shelf near you, delivered as easily as walking into the mall used to be,” DoorDash Chief Revenue Officer Shanna Prevé said in the release. “You can get Macy’s or Anthropologie in as little as an hour and return it just as easily if it’s not right, no box, no label, back on the shelf and the money back in your pocket. For retailers, it means turning the stores they already have into a growth channel, not a warehouse three states away.”

The returns are possible via Dasher Returns, which lets consumers pay a flat $7.99 fee to schedule a return for an eligible retail order, and a Dasher can retrieve it from their door in as quickly as 30 minutes and bring it back to the store, according to the release. Pricing and times are subject to change.
“The return is processed on the spot, the item can go directly back on the shelf, and the consumer receives their refund within days,” the release said.
DoorDash also announced several other products and services Wednesday as it held its Dash Forward 2026 event.
These include the ability to place orders with DoorDash by sending a text rather than using an app or browser; the ability to connect DoorDash to compatible internal AI tools so employees can order team lunches or items for office restocking; a platform called DoorDash OS that connects all the DoorDash tools that are used by restaurants; a new AI assistant called DashBuddy that answers questions for Dashers; and a planned upcoming drone delivery system that will serve local businesses, the company said in several press releases issued Wednesday.
DoorDash last week announced a drone delivery partnership with Lowe’s and Google’s Wing, PYMNTS reported Thursday (Sept. 24).
The move and others like it are giving retailers a way to find out what delivery speed is worth, PYMNTS reported Friday (Sept. 25). More than 20% of orders on the DoorDash platform last year traveled between three and five miles, but those orders took almost 25% longer than shorter deliveries, mainly because pairing them with a driver took longer. Drone-delivered orders arrived in an average of 25 minutes during 2025, while some locations taking part in partner drone pilots saw order volumes grow by around 30%.
“Whether the arithmetic works will depend heavily on cost,” the report said, citing Barclays research showing autonomous delivery costs below that of conventional delivery. “Cutting several dollars from fulfillment does more to improve the economics of delivering a $15 order than a $150 order.”

Whether you are buying kibble for a pet or ordering takeout for dinner, you likely interact with digital giants Chewy (CHWY +4.87%) and DoorDash (DASH -0.96%). But which is the better buy?
Chewy dominates the online pet supplies market with a subscription-heavy model that ensures predictable revenue. DoorDash serves as a logistics backbone for local delivery across diverse retail categories. Both companies utilize massive logistics networks to capture consumer spending, though their paths to profitability and valuation multiples vary significantly for investors.
Chewy has established itself as a leader among retail stocks by focusing exclusively on the pet category. The company sells food, supplies, and medications primarily through its website and mobile apps, serving over 21 million active customers. Its strategy relies heavily on the Autoship subscription program, which simplifies repeat purchases for pet parents and provides the business with high revenue visibility. Recently, the company expanded into physical services through Chewy Vet Care clinics and the acquisition of Modern Animal to deepen its relationship with customers.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $12.6 billion, representing a growth rate of approximately 6.2% compared to the prior year. This steady increase in sales helped the company achieve net income of close to $222.8 million. While the net margin remains relatively thin at roughly 1.8%, the move into positive territory highlights a transition from early-stage expansion to a more mature and profitable operation. This stability is vital for investors looking for consistent performance in the specialty retail industry.
As of its February 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 1.0x, which means its total debt is roughly equal to its shareholder equity. Its current ratio, a measure of a company's ability to cover its short-term debts with assets it expects to convert to cash within a year, is nearly 0.9x. In fiscal year 2025, the company generated free cash flow of approximately $562.4 million, which is calculated as cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 43.1% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since it is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
DoorDash operates a massive local commerce platform that connects merchants, consumers, and delivery workers across more than 40 countries. While it began with restaurant delivery, it has expanded into grocery stores, convenience stores, and other retail categories. The company leverages its DashPass membership program, which exceeded 35 million members by the end of 2025, to drive customer loyalty and more frequent orders. In addition to delivery commissions, the company generates revenue through advertising solutions for its merchant partners, creating a diversified income stream.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $13.7 billion, showing robust growth of approximately 27.9% over the previous year. This rapid expansion was accompanied by a significant improvement in profitability, as the company reported net income of roughly $935.0 million. Its net margin reached approximately 6.8%, a substantial rise from previous years when the company was still reporting losses. The combination of high double-digit revenue growth and expanding profitability makes it a compelling option for those seeking momentum in the tech-enabled logistics space.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x, indicating that total debt is much lower than shareholder equity. Its current ratio stands at nearly 1.4x, suggesting a strong ability to meet short-term financial obligations. The company generated impressive free cash flow of close to $1.8 billion in fiscal 2025. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 43.2% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation because this non-cash expense is added back during the accounting process.
Chewy faces intense competition from e-commerce giants and large mass retailers. It specifically faces pressure from Amazon, which competes on price and delivery speed across the pet category. Operational risks include potential disruptions to its complex fulfillment network and a heavy reliance on third-party cloud infrastructure providers. Furthermore, the company must navigate strict legal and regulatory compliance requirements related to its pharmacy and veterinary services, where non-compliance could lead to significant sanctions or the loss of operating licenses.
DoorDash faces significant legal and regulatory challenges, particularly regarding the classification of its delivery drivers as independent contractors. Changes in labor laws could force the company to reclassify these workers, which would materially increase costs and complicate its operating model. The market for local delivery is also highly competitive, with Delivery Hero and other logistics platforms fighting for market share. Additionally, as the company processes vast amounts of sensitive personal data, it remains a target for cybersecurity attacks that could damage its brand reputation and lead to costly litigation.
Chewy offers a lower valuation through its P/S ratio, which measures market cap divided by sales over the past twelve months, while DoorDash trades at a higher Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Chewy and DoorDash both operate in the digital commerce and delivery spaces, taking products from order pages to customers' doorsteps. But as consumers battle ever-higher prices for basics like gas and groceries, can Chewy and DoorDash continue their growth trajectories? In the current economic environment, I'm looking at which company can keep customers coming back.
DoorDash is nearly 10 times the size of Chewy by market cap, and it's still growing much faster. It can use its blistering revenue growth to invest in improving its digital logistics network, which drives more orders and DashPass sign-ups. DashPass is the thing to watch here, as it can be a helpful measure of DoorDash's customer retention. In the second quarter, DashPass customers generated 75% of U.S. grocery and retail orders. DoorDash will report Q3 results on Nov. 4.
Chewy stock dropped 11% after its Q2 earnings release in September despite solid revenue growth as management pointed to continued pressure for the pet industry, evidenced by fewer treat and other discretionary sales. But it isn't all treats and toys at Chewy. While it continues to expand its pet health services, it also maintains a robust roster of Autoship customers, who comprise nearly 85% of its sales. The bulk of these sales come from consumables including food and medication, which aren't negotiable for pet owners.
Autoship sales jumped modestly year over year and net sales per active customer continued to increase in Q2. Despite its slower growth, I like Chewy as a more defensive play against a challenging consumer landscape. Plus, with the stock nearly cut in half over the past year, and valuations either lower than or in line with the broader industry average, Chewy stock may have room for a big improvement over the next year or so, provided it maintains or improves operational efficiency and keeps its loyal customers happy.

pages.title: DoorDash sued over alleged sexual assault in South Florida apartment
pages.text:
Woman sues DoorDash, says driver assaulted her after vodka delivery
The lawsuit claims DoorDash's alcohol delivery rules put customers at risk.
A Palm Beach County woman is suing DoorDash after she was allegedly sexually assaulted by a delivery driver.
The lawsuit claims the driver entered her home to verify her age for an alcohol delivery and then forced her to perform oral sex.
DoorDash, in response, said it has zero tolerance for violence and is taking the allegations seriously.
A Palm Beach County woman is suing the food-delivery giant DoorDash over allegations that a driver sexually assaulted her in the entryway of her apartment.
The woman, identified in the lawsuit only as Jane Doe, said she ordered a bottle of vodka to her house on a Saturday night in March. She said the deliveryman entered her home under the guise of verifying her age, then pushed her to her knees and forced her to perform oral sex.
"DoorDash takes these allegations seriously and has zero tolerance for violence of any kind on the platform," Jenn Rosenberg, a DoorDash spokesperson, said Tuesday.
Filed Oct. 8 in West Palm Beach, the lawsuit doesn't say whether the assault was reported to or investigated by authorities, nor whether criminal charges are pending. It also omits the name of the accused driver, though Doe's Miami-based attorney Donevan Mallard said he plans to add the name once he and his client learn it.
Until then, Mallard referred to the deliveryman as John Doe and said his actions hurt his client physically, psychologically and emotionally. Mallard said the woman was humiliated by the incident and has incurred medical and counseling expenses as a result of it.
In the lawsuit, the attorney said DoorDash had a responsibility to make sure drivers entrusted with customers' addresses are safe and trustworthy. He argues that the company failed to investigate the driver's background adequately, including any criminal history, and failed to monitor him after letting him onto the platform.
The lawsuit also takes aim at the company's procedures for alcohol deliveries.
Mallard said that by requiring customers to interact with drivers to verify their age, DoorDash created a situation with foreseeable safety risks. The attorney said the company should have instructed customers that drivers do not need to enter their homes and should have trained drivers to complete alcohol verification at the doorway or another safe location.
The lawsuit contains several claims: battery and sexual battery against the unidentified driver, and three negligence claims against DoorDash over the driver's selection, his continued supervision and the company's alcohol-delivery safety procedures.
Jane Doe is seeking more than $50,000 in damages and has requested a jury trial.

What Happened?
A number of stocks fell in the afternoon session after the major indices pulled back and tech-oriented equities fell as the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported a hotter-than-expected September inflation print, pushing Treasury yields higher.
As detailed by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the consumer price index rose 3.7% year-over-year in September, topping the 3.6% estimate from economists polled by Dow Jones. Financial analysts explain that higher benchmark yields mechanically elevate the discount rate applied to corporate earnings, compressing the multiples investors are willing to pay for equities. Chewy vs. DoorDash: As Consumers Tighten Their Wallets, Which Stock Can Thrive?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 2:40 PM CDT 7 min read
Whether you are buying kibble for a pet or ordering takeout for dinner, you likely interact with digital giants Chewy (NYSE:CHWY) and DoorDash (NASDAQ:DASH). But which is the better buy?
Chewy dominates the online pet supplies market with a subscription-heavy model that ensures predictable revenue. DoorDash serves as a logistics backbone for local delivery across diverse retail categories. Both companies utilize massive logistics networks to capture consumer spending, though their paths to profitability and valuation multiples vary significantly for investors.
Chewy has established itself as a leader among retail stocks by focusing exclusively on the pet category. The company sells food, supplies, and medications primarily through its website and mobile apps, serving over 21 million active customers. Its strategy relies heavily on the Autoship subscription program, which simplifies repeat purchases for pet parents and provides the business with high revenue visibility. Recently, the company expanded into physical services through Chewy Vet Care clinics and the acquisition of Modern Animal to deepen its relationship with customers.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $12.6 billion, representing a growth rate of approximately 6.2% compared to the prior year. This steady increase in sales helped the company achieve net income of close to $222.8 million. While the net margin remains relatively thin at roughly 1.8%, the move into positive territory highlights a transition from early-stage expansion to a more mature and profitable operation. This stability is vital for investors looking for consistent performance in the specialty retail industry.
As of its February 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 1.0x, which means its total debt is roughly equal to its shareholder equity. Its current ratio, a measure of a company's ability to cover its short-term debts with assets it expects to convert to cash within a year, is nearly 0.9x. In fiscal year 2025, the company generated free cash flow of approximately $562.4 million, which is calculated as cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 43.1% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since it is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
DoorDash operates a massive local commerce platform that connects merchants, consumers, and delivery workers across more than 40 countries. While it began with restaurant delivery, it has expanded into grocery stores, convenience stores, and other retail categories. The company leverages its DashPass membership program, which exceeded 35 million members by the end of 2025, to drive customer loyalty and more frequent orders. In addition to delivery commissions, the company generates revenue through advertising solutions for its merchant partners, creating a diversified income stream.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $13.7 billion, showing robust growth of approximately 27.9% over the previous year. This rapid expansion was accompanied by a significant improvement in profitability, as the company reported net income of roughly $935.0 million. Its net margin reached approximately 6.8%, a substantial rise from previous years when the company was still reporting losses. The combination of high double-digit revenue growth and expanding profitability makes it a compelling option for those seeking momentum in the tech-enabled logistics space.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x, indicating that total debt is much lower than shareholder equity. Its current ratio stands at nearly 1.4x, suggesting a strong ability to meet short-term financial obligations. The company generated impressive free cash flow of close to $1.8 billion in fiscal 2025. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 43.2% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation because this non-cash expense is added back during the accounting process.
Chewy faces intense competition from e-commerce giants and large mass retailers. It specifically faces pressure from Amazon, which competes on price and delivery speed across the pet category. Operational risks include potential disruptions to its complex fulfillment network and a heavy reliance on third-party cloud infrastructure providers. Furthermore, the company must navigate strict legal and regulatory compliance requirements related to its pharmacy and veterinary services, where non-compliance could lead to significant sanctions or the loss of operating licenses.
DoorDash faces significant legal and regulatory challenges, particularly regarding the classification of its delivery drivers as independent contractors. Changes in labor laws could force the company to reclassify these workers, which would materially increase costs and complicate its operating model. The market for local delivery is also highly competitive, with Delivery Hero and other logistics platforms fighting for market share. Additionally, as the company processes vast amounts of sensitive personal data, it remains a target for cybersecurity attacks that could damage its brand reputation and lead to costly litigation.
Chewy offers a lower valuation through its P/S ratio, which measures market cap divided by sales over the past twelve months, while DoorDash trades at a higher Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Chewy and DoorDash both operate in the digital commerce and delivery spaces, taking products from order pages to customers' doorsteps. But as consumers battle ever-higher prices for basics like gas and groceries, can Chewy and DoorDash continue their growth trajectories? In the current economic environment, I'm looking at which company can keep customers coming back.
DoorDash is nearly 10 times the size of Chewy by market cap, and it's still growing much faster. It can use its blistering revenue growth to invest in improving its digital logistics network, which drives more orders and DashPass sign-ups. DashPass is the thing to watch here, as it can be a helpful measure of DoorDash's customer retention. In the second quarter, DashPass customers generated 75% of U.S. grocery and retail orders. DoorDash will report Q3 results on Nov. 4.
Chewy stock dropped 11% after its Q2 earnings release in September despite solid revenue growth as management pointed to continued pressure for the pet industry, evidenced by fewer treat and other discretionary sales. But it isn't all treats and toys at Chewy. While it continues to expand its pet health services, it also maintains a robust roster of Autoship customers, who comprise nearly 85% of its sales. The bulk of these sales come from consumables including food and medication, which aren't negotiable for pet owners.
Autoship sales jumped modestly year over year and net sales per active customer continued to increase in Q2. Despite its slower growth, I like Chewy as a more defensive play against a challenging consumer landscape. Plus, with the stock nearly cut in half over the past year, and valuations either lower than or in line with the broader industry average, Chewy stock may have room for a big improvement over the next year or so, provided it maintains or improves operational efficiency and keeps its loyal customers happy.

Chewy vs. DoorDash: As Consumers Tighten Their Wallets, Which Stock Can Thrive?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 2:40 PM CDT 7 min read
Whether you are buying kibble for a pet or ordering takeout for dinner, you likely interact with digital giants Chewy (NYSE:CHWY) and DoorDash (NASDAQ:DASH). But which is the better buy?
Chewy dominates the online pet supplies market with a subscription-heavy model that ensures predictable revenue. DoorDash serves as a logistics backbone for local delivery across diverse retail categories. Both companies utilize massive logistics networks to capture consumer spending, though their paths to profitability and valuation multiples vary significantly for investors.
Chewy has established itself as a leader among retail stocks by focusing exclusively on the pet category. The company sells food, supplies, and medications primarily through its website and mobile apps, serving over 21 million active customers. Its strategy relies heavily on the Autoship subscription program, which simplifies repeat purchases for pet parents and provides the business with high revenue visibility. Recently, the company expanded into physical services through Chewy Vet Care clinics and the acquisition of Modern Animal to deepen its relationship with customers.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $12.6 billion, representing a growth rate of approximately 6.2% compared to the prior year. This steady increase in sales helped the company achieve net income of close to $222.8 million. While the net margin remains relatively thin at roughly 1.8%, the move into positive territory highlights a transition from early-stage expansion to a more mature and profitable operation. This stability is vital for investors looking for consistent performance in the specialty retail industry.
As of its February 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 1.0x, which means its total debt is roughly equal to its shareholder equity. Its current ratio, a measure of a company's ability to cover its short-term debts with assets it expects to convert to cash within a year, is nearly 0.9x. In fiscal year 2025, the company generated free cash flow of approximately $562.4 million, which is calculated as cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 43.1% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since it is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
DoorDash operates a massive local commerce platform that connects merchants, consumers, and delivery workers across more than 40 countries. While it began with restaurant delivery, it has expanded into grocery stores, convenience stores, and other retail categories. The company leverages its DashPass membership program, which exceeded 35 million members by the end of 2025, to drive customer loyalty and more frequent orders. In addition to delivery commissions, the company generates revenue through advertising solutions for its merchant partners, creating a diversified income stream.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $13.7 billion, showing robust growth of approximately 27.9% over the previous year. This rapid expansion was accompanied by a significant improvement in profitability, as the company reported net income of roughly $935.0 million. Its net margin reached approximately 6.8%, a substantial rise from previous years when the company was still reporting losses. The combination of high double-digit revenue growth and expanding profitability makes it a compelling option for those seeking momentum in the tech-enabled logistics space.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x, indicating that total debt is much lower than shareholder equity. Its current ratio stands at nearly 1.4x, suggesting a strong ability to meet short-term financial obligations. The company generated impressive free cash flow of close to $1.8 billion in fiscal 2025. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 43.2% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation because this non-cash expense is added back during the accounting process.
Chewy faces intense competition from e-commerce giants and large mass retailers. It specifically faces pressure from Amazon, which competes on price and delivery speed across the pet category. Operational risks include potential disruptions to its complex fulfillment network and a heavy reliance on third-party cloud infrastructure providers. Furthermore, the company must navigate strict legal and regulatory compliance requirements related to its pharmacy and veterinary services, where non-compliance could lead to significant sanctions or the loss of operating licenses.
DoorDash faces significant legal and regulatory challenges, particularly regarding the classification of its delivery drivers as independent contractors. Changes in labor laws could force the company to reclassify these workers, which would materially increase costs and complicate its operating model. The market for local delivery is also highly competitive, with Delivery Hero and other logistics platforms fighting for market share. Additionally, as the company processes vast amounts of sensitive personal data, it remains a target for cybersecurity attacks that could damage its brand reputation and lead to costly litigation.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Chewy and DoorDash both operate in the digital commerce and delivery spaces, taking products from order pages to customers' doorsteps. But as consumers battle ever-higher prices for basics like gas and groceries, can Chewy and DoorDash continue their growth trajectories? In the current economic environment, I'm looking at which company can keep customers coming back.
DoorDash is nearly 10 times the size of Chewy by market cap, and it's still growing much faster. It can use its blistering revenue growth to invest in improving its digital logistics network, which drives more orders and DashPass sign-ups. DashPass is the thing to watch here, as it can be a helpful measure of DoorDash's customer retention. In the second quarter, DashPass customers generated 75% of U.S. grocery and retail orders. DoorDash will report Q3 results on Nov. 4.
Chewy stock dropped 11% after its Q2 earnings release in September despite solid revenue growth as management pointed to continued pressure for the pet industry, evidenced by fewer treat and other discretionary sales. But it isn't all treats and toys at Chewy. While it continues to expand its pet health services, it also maintains a robust roster of Autoship customers, who comprise nearly 85% of its sales. The bulk of these sales come from consumables including food and medication, which aren't negotiable for pet owners.
Autoship sales jumped modestly year over year and net sales per active customer continued to increase in Q2. Despite its slower growth, I like Chewy as a more defensive play against a challenging consumer landscape. Plus, with the stock nearly cut in half over the past year, and valuations either lower than or in line with the broader industry average, Chewy stock may have room for a big improvement over the next year or so, provided it maintains or improves operational efficiency and keeps its loyal customers happy.
